lead: When there are too many options to compare, freedom of choice can turn into a burden.
when: When the more you shop the more confused you get, when you keep putting off starting a course, or when you keep comparing options after you've already decided, this is a good one to use.
body:
You open a food delivery app and half an hour later you still haven't picked anything. You go to buy toothpaste, and the more specs you read, the more you worry about missing a better one. The paradox of choice says that in some situations, more options make it harder to get started and more likely you'll regret your pick afterward. That's because you're not only judging each option; you also keep imagining the ones you gave up.

The paradox of choice holds that under certain conditions, adding options can increase the burden of comparison, delay decisions, and lower satisfaction, though this kind of choice overload doesn't show up in every situation.

Not everyone dislikes lots of options, though. Someone who knows cameras well may enjoy a wide range, while a beginner just wants to know which few suit them. What matters is whether you have a goal, criteria for comparing, and a point where you can stop searching, not just the total number of options.

Think of choosing as a funnel that opens up and then narrows: first accept that there are many possibilities, then use clear criteria to rule out the ones that don't fit, and finally compare a small number of candidates. Narrowing down is about easing the work of comparing, not cutting things at random until only one is left.
example:
You want an ordinary office chair. At first you only care that it's comfortable and reasonably priced. After a week of reading reviews, you start worrying about every detail: armrests, materials, mesh, the base. The more you research, the less you dare to order.

Go back to how you'll actually use it: how many hours a day you sit, where you feel uncomfortable, what your budget is, and whether you can try it or return it. Narrow it down to three chairs that meet your basic needs, actually try them, then decide by a set time. The goal is to get a chair that works for you, not to prove there's no better one anywhere on the market.
extra: When you're meeting friends for dinner, asking "what do you want to eat?" can drag on forever. Asking "noodles, hot pot, or something light?" first, and then picking a specific place based on what people can't eat, often makes it much easier. Cutting down how many comparisons people face at once works better than deciding for everyone.
steps: Decide on your two or three most important needs, plus the budget or time you won't go beyond.
Use those criteria to narrow things down to a few comparable options, and stop adding new candidates.
Set a "this is good enough" standard, and let yourself stop searching once something meets it.
caution: Fewer options aren't always better. When the differences are real and the information is clear, a wide choice can be very valuable. And don't hide alternatives that matter to other people just to make things simpler.
exercise: For one decision you're stuck on, set three requirements, at most three candidates, and a deadline. When time's up, choose based on your requirements, and don't keep postponing because "maybe there's something better."
brief: From an explosion of branches to a focused decision: on the left, a stick figure faces branches fanning out into many nearly identical cups, with tangled lines above its head; on the right, the options are filtered first so only a few distinguishable cups remain, and the stick figure can compare them more easily.
diagramCaption: First open up the possibilities, then use clear criteria to narrow them down to a few candidates.
